items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Groundwater stored in aquifers for thousands of years that is not significantly recharged today"?
items.answer: fossil water
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of fossil water.

items.stem: Explain why desalination illustrates trade-offs within the nexus.
items.answer: It increases water security in arid countries (Israel, Saudi Arabia) but uses large amounts of energy - often from fossil fuels - raising emissions and costs, and produces brine waste.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It increases water security in arid countries (Israel, Saudi Arabia) but uses large amounts of energy - often from fossil fuels - raising emissions and costs, and produces brine waste. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between energy security and water security.
items.answer: Water security is reliable access to sufficient safe water for people, economy and ecosystems; energy security is reliable, affordable access to energy supplies, including resilience to supply disruption.
items.markingKey: Water security is reliable access to sufficient safe water for people, economy and ecosystems; energy security is reliable, affordable access to energy supplies, including resilience to supply disruption. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: FAO AQUASTAT lists total renewable freshwater for Egypt as roughly 57.5 km³/yr; the population is approximately 112.7 million. Calculate the renewable water available per person (m³ per year) and classify it using the Falkenmark indicator (1,700 / 1,000 / 500 m³).
items.answer: 510 m³ per person per year: water scarcity
items.markingKey: M1 conversion (1 km³ = 10⁹ m³); A1 510; R1 water scarcity.

items.stem: A student claims: "Hydropower has no effect on food production." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Dams can flood farmland, alter fisheries and sediment supply to deltas (e.g. the Mekong), affecting food production downstream.
items.markingKey: Dams can flood farmland, alter fisheries and sediment supply to deltas (e.g. the Mekong), affecting food production downstream. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

Explain what the data suggest about energy choices in water-scarce regions.
items.answer: Solar PV and wind use very little water, so they increase energy security without competing with water for food; thermal plants add water stress.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that integrated management of the water-food-energy nexus is essential for resource security.
items.answer: Integration is essential in principle, though practical progress requires coordinated institutions and pricing.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: interdependence means single-resource policies create trade-offs (biofuels, Punjab); integrated planning can find synergies (solar irrigation, wastewater reuse). Against / limitations: integrated approaches are complex and institutions are divided by sector; some issues are best solved by targeted policies. A supported conclusion might be: Integration is essential in principle, though practical progress requires coordinated institutions and pricing. items.stem: "Energy security is the most important element of the nexus." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Each element is critical; energy often acts as the lever, but water is the fundamental constraint in many regions.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: energy enables water supply and modern farming; energy shocks (2022) raised fertiliser and food prices. items.stem: Explain how free electricity for irrigation can undermine resource security.
items.answer: It encourages over-pumping of groundwater, lowering water tables, raising energy demand and costs to the state, and threatening future food production, as in Punjab.

items.stem: Suggest how solar-powered irrigation pumps could affect the water-food-energy nexus in India.
items.answer: They provide cheap, low-carbon energy for irrigation, raising yields, but zero marginal cost may encourage over-extraction unless farmers can sell surplus power to the grid.
items.markingKey: They provide cheap, low-carbon energy for irrigation, raising yields, but zero marginal cost may encourage over-extraction unless farmers can sell surplus power to the grid.

items.answer: physical water scarcity

items.stem: Distinguish between physical water scarcity and economic water scarcity.
items.answer: Physical scarcity means there is insufficient water to meet demand (e.g. Middle East, North Africa); economic scarcity means water exists but people lack infrastructure or money to access it (e.g. much of sub-Saharan Africa).
items.markingKey: Physical scarcity means there is insufficient water to meet demand (e.g. Middle East, North Africa); economic scarcity means water exists but people lack infrastructure or money to access it (e.g. much of sub-Saharan Africa). items.stem: Explain how virtual water trade can improve water security in arid countries.
items.answer: By importing water-intensive goods such as wheat and beef, countries like Jordan and Egypt avoid using scarce domestic water to grow them, effectively importing water embedded in food.

items.answer: Demand was cut by about half to around 500 million litres a day and Day Zero was avoided. Restrictions, pricing and public awareness can rapidly cut urban water use.

items.stem: Examine the view that virtual water trade increases global water security.
items.answer: Virtual water trade helps when exporters are water-rich, but can shift stress to vulnerable exporters.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "water stress"?

When there is not enough water to meet all demands, including environmental flows, as in arid regions
When annual renewable water supplies fall below about 1,700 m³ per person (Falkenmark indicator)
The uninterrupted availability of energy sources at an affordable price (IEA)
items.answer: When annual renewable water supplies fall below about 1,700 m³ per person (Falkenmark indicator)

items.answer: It is energy-intensive and costly, produces brine and is most practical for wealthy coastal states; inland and poor regions cannot rely on it.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "undernourishment"?
options: When water is available but lack of investment, infrastructure or institutions prevents people from accessing it
The date on which a city's taps would be turned off because reservoirs are too low, a term popularised in Cape Town in 2018
When all people at all times have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food (FAO, 1996)
A condition in which a person's regular food intake is insufficient to provide the dietary energy needed for a normal, active, healthy life
items.answer: A condition in which a person's regular food intake is insufficient to provide the dietary energy needed for a normal, active, healthy life

items.answer: About a third of food produced is lost or wasted; better storage and cold chains in low-income countries and reduced retail/household waste in high-income countries would increase supply and lower prices.

items.stem: Examine the interactions between water, food and energy security, with reference to examples.
items.answer: Indicative content: Nexus explained with flows; named examples (Saudi wheat, Punjab, biofuels, GERD, desalination); trade-offs and synergies; judgement.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Nexus explained with flows; named examples (Saudi wheat, Punjab, biofuels, GERD, desalination); trade-offs and synergies; judgement. Paper 1 extended-response markbands [10]: 9-10 responds to all demands of the question; accurate, detailed knowledge and understanding; well-developed, relevant examples and case studies with specific (named, located, quantified) detail; balanced, well-structured evaluation leading to a substantiated conclusion. 7-8 responds to most demands; mostly accurate knowledge; examples relevant but not always fully developed; evaluation present but uneven. 5-6 some demands addressed; knowledge partly accurate; examples general or loosely linked; evaluation mostly implicit. 3-4 limited, largely descriptive; little use of examples. 1-2 little relevant knowledge or understanding. 0 does not reach the standard of the descriptors.

items.stem: "Technology offers the best solution to water insecurity." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Technology is powerful for wealthy states, but governance, pricing and demand reduction are more widely applicable.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: desalination and recycling transformed Israel and Singapore; drip irrigation increases efficiency. Arguments challenging it: high cost and energy use limit access for poor countries; demand management, pricing and governance address root causes. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Technology is powerful for wealthy states, but governance, pricing and demand reduction are more widely applicable. Paper 2 Section C markbands [15]: 13-15 thorough response to all demands including the command term; accurate, detailed geographical knowledge and terminology; well-chosen, located and quantified examples at more than one scale; explicit, balanced evaluation (perspectives, places, scales, time) with a well-substantiated conclusion. 10-12 most demands addressed; accurate knowledge; examples relevant and developed; evaluation is balanced but not sustained. 7-9 some demands addressed; knowledge mostly accurate; examples partly developed; evaluation partial or one-sided. 4-6 limited, mainly descriptive; generalised examples; little evaluation. 1-3 little relevant knowledge; no examples or evaluation. 0 does not reach the standard of the descriptors.

items.stem: "Poverty, rather than food production, is the main cause of food insecurity." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Poverty is the dominant underlying cause, but conflict and climate increasingly drive acute hunger.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: global calorie supply exceeds needs; most hungry people are poor rural households; price spikes harm access (2008). Arguments challenging it: low yields and climate shocks reduce availability in the Sahel; conflict causes most famines (Somalia, Yemen, Sudan). Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Poverty is the dominant underlying cause, but conflict and climate increasingly drive acute hunger. items.stem: Examine the view that geopolitics is the main threat to energy security.
items.answer: Geopolitics causes the most dramatic shocks, but physical and economic factors also threaten security.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: 2022 Russian gas cuts, Hormuz tensions, 1973 oil embargo; chokepoints and pipeline politics. Against / limitations: extreme weather (Texas 2021 freeze), underinvestment and demand growth; energy poverty reflects low incomes and infrastructure. A supported conclusion might be: Geopolitics causes the most dramatic shocks, but physical and economic factors also threaten security. items.stem: Approximately what share of the US maize harvest is used to make ethanol?
items.answer: About 35-40%
items.markingKey: D. The Renewable Fuel Standard drives demand; critics link biofuels to the 2007-08 food price spike.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "Day Zero".
items.answer: The date on which a city's taps would be turned off because reservoirs are too low, a term popularised in Cape Town in 2018
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the date on which a city's taps would be turned off because reservoirs are too low, a term popularised in Cape Town in 2018. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: What are the four dimensions (pillars) of food security?
items.answer: Availability, access, utilisation and stability
items.markingKey: Availability, access, utilisation and stability. The FAO framework distinguishes these four pillars.

items.stem: A student claims: "Countries with large fossil-fuel reserves are always energy secure." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Exporters may lack refining capacity (Nigeria imported petrol), and energy poverty can coexist with large reserves.
items.markingKey: Exporters may lack refining capacity (Nigeria imported petrol), and energy poverty can coexist with large reserves. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Increasing energy supply always improves water security." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Some energy sources (coal, nuclear, biofuels, hydropower) use or divert large amounts of water, so energy expansion can reduce water availability.
items.markingKey: Some energy sources (coal, nuclear, biofuels, hydropower) use or divert large amounts of water, so energy expansion can reduce water availability. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between blue water and green water.
items.answer: Blue water is surface and groundwater used for irrigation and supply; green water is rainwater stored in soil and used by plants, the main source for rain-fed crops.
items.markingKey: Blue water is surface and groundwater used for irrigation and supply; green water is rainwater stored in soil and used by plants, the main source for rain-fed crops. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why land grabbing is controversial.
items.answer: Investors gain land, water and exports, but local farmers and pastoralists may lose customary land without consent, food may be exported from food-insecure countries, and benefits (jobs, infrastructure) are often smaller than promised.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Investors gain land, water and exports, but local farmers and pastoralists may lose customary land without consent, food may be exported from food-insecure countries, and benefits (jobs, infrastructure) are often smaller than promised. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Renewable energy removes all energy security risks." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Renewables reduce fuel import risks but create risks of intermittency and dependence on critical minerals and foreign manufacturing.
items.markingKey: Renewables reduce fuel import risks but create risks of intermittency and dependence on critical minerals and foreign manufacturing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Resource security problems can be solved one resource at a time." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Because of the nexus, solving one problem can worsen another (e.g. biofuels for energy raising food prices); integrated policies are needed.
items.markingKey: Because of the nexus, solving one problem can worsen another (e.g. biofuels for energy raising food prices); integrated policies are needed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Water Footprint Network averages: cup of coffee 130 L per cup, chicken meat 4,300 L per kg. Calculate the virtual water embedded in a weekly purchase by a café in Melbourne of 6 cup of coffee, 2 kg of chicken meat.
items.answer: 9,380 litres
items.markingKey: M1 multiplying each quantity by its water content; A1 9,380 L.

items.stem: A cooperative growing sorghum in Burkina Faso harvested 48,738 t from 8,714 ha in 2005 and 36,001 t from the same area in 2020. Calculate the yield (t/ha) in each year and the percentage change in yield. Suggest two reasons for the change.
items.answer: 5.59 t/ha → 4.13 t/ha; -26.1%; e.g. improved seeds/fertiliser/irrigation (if rising) or drought, soil degradation, pests (if falling).
items.markingKey: A1 5.59, A1 4.13, A1 -26.1%. R1 R1 two reasons consistent with the direction.

items.stem: Briefly describe China's "Malacca dilemma" and explain what it reveals about chokepoints and energy security.
items.answer: About 80% of China's oil imports pass through the Strait of Malacca. Dependence on one shipping route encourages pipelines through Myanmar and Central Asia and the Belt and Road Initiative.
items.markingKey: Context (About 80% of China's oil imports pass through the Strait of Malacca.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Dependence on one shipping route encourages pipelines through Myanmar and Central Asia and the Belt and Road Initiative. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to chokepoints and energy security.

items.stem: Water Footprint Network averages: cup of coffee 130 L per cup, beef 15,400 L per kg, cheese 3,200 L per kg. Calculate the virtual water embedded in a weekly purchase by a household in Madrid of 5 cup of coffee, 5 kg of beef, 5 kg of cheese. Explain why virtual water trade matters for water-scarce importing countries.
items.answer: 93,650 litres; importing water-intensive goods lets scarce countries (e.g. Jordan, Egypt) "save" domestic water, but creates dependence on exporters.
items.markingKey: M1 multiplying each quantity by its water content; A1 93,650 L. R1 virtual-water explanation.

items.stem: Using a named city, outline two strategies used to manage a water crisis.
items.answer: e.g. Cape Town 2018: restricting use to 50 L per person per day with tariffs and public dashboards; pressure management and leak repair; new groundwater and small desalination plants.
items.markingKey: e.g. Cape Town 2018: restricting use to 50 L per person per day with tariffs and public dashboards; pressure management and leak repair; new groundwater and small desalination plants.

items.stem: Using famine in Somalia (2011) as an example, explain the role of conflict and governance in food insecurity.
items.answer: Drought, conflict and restricted humanitarian access led to about 260,000 deaths. Drought became famine because conflict blocked markets and aid.
items.markingKey: Context (Drought, conflict and restricted humanitarian access led to about 260,000 deaths.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Drought became famine because conflict blocked markets and aid. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of conflict and governance in food insecurity.

items.stem: Briefly describe France's nuclear programme and explain what it reveals about policy responses to energy insecurity.
items.answer: The Messmer Plan after the 1973 oil crisis gave France about 56 reactors producing about 65-70% of its electricity. A state-led shift to domestic nuclear generation reduced reliance on imported oil.
items.markingKey: Context (The Messmer Plan after the 1973 oil crisis gave France about 56 reactors producing about 65-70% of its electricity.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A state-led shift to domestic nuclear generation reduced reliance on imported oil. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to policy responses to energy insecurity.

items.stem: Give one strength and one weakness of the claim that integrated management of the water-food-energy nexus is essential for resource security.
items.answer: Integration is essential in principle, though practical progress requires coordinated institutions and pricing.
items.markingKey: For: interdependence means single-resource policies create trade-offs (biofuels, Punjab). Against: integrated approaches are complex and institutions are divided by sector. [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Text: "Japan imports about 88% of its primary energy. After the 2011 Fukushima disaster, the share of nuclear in electricity fell from about 25% to almost zero, and LNG imports rose by about a quarter."

(a) Explain why Japan is described as energy insecure. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest one consequence of the fall in nuclear output. [6]
items.answer: (a) It has very few domestic fossil resources and imports nearly 90% of its energy, mostly by sea, so is vulnerable to price and supply shocks. (b) Higher fuel import bills and trade deficits, higher electricity prices and higher CO₂ emissions from gas and coal plants.
items.markingKey: (a) It has very few domestic fossil resources and imports nearly 90% of its energy, mostly by sea, so is vulnerable to price and supply shocks. (b) Higher fuel import bills and trade deficits, higher electricity prices and higher CO₂ emissions from gas and coal plants. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). Infographic markscheme [10]: part (a) [4] - award 1 mark per valid point taken from the resource (data must be quoted with units for full marks); part (b) [6] - up to 2 marks for each developed explanation linking the resource to own knowledge; reward named examples; maximum 3 marks if the resource is not used.
